title: Practical exam – subjects (summaries)
html:
Source: Exam subjects Final.pdf – summaries of the practical (lab) exam subjects

1. Measurement of visual acuity

Visual acuity (VA) refers to the eye's ability to distinguish the shapes and details of objects at a certain distance, being a

measurement of central vision only.

= an essential component of visual function, being dependent on the normal functioning of complex processes:

stimulation of the retina by light, appropriate refraction, retinal health, ability of the optical pathways to conduct visual

information, and correct cortical interpretation of visual stimuli.

Required equipment:

- Optotype for distance: wall chart with rows of printed numbers/letters/signs.

The symbols are large at the top and get smaller in each row as we look down the chart

- Optotype for near

- Pinhole: black screen w/ a central hole that allows light rays to reach the retina, correcting the eye's optical problems

Stages of examination

VA is measured immediately after history-taking and before the objective examination, because:

▪ It quickly provides an overview of the severity of the ophthalmic condition

▪ Objective exam involves projecting light into the eyes + instilling mydriatic drops, which temporarily decrease VA.

Measuring Distance VA:

▪ Pt is seated comfortably, 5m away from the optotype, with distance glasses, if they normally use them.

One eye is covered and the patient is asked to read the smallest line they can see. The lowest row that the patient can

correctly read is noted:

Example: if the patient can only read the first row, which should be seen from 50m, the VA will be 5/50 = 0.1

▪ The patient is asked to read through a hole (pinhole) to see if this improves vision.

=> If vision is improved through the pinhole = refractive error responsible for pt's decreased VA

Normal VA = 1(10/10, 20/20) = Emmetropia

Recording VA:

The VA is recorded as the ratio btwn the distance at which the optotype is located (5m) / the distance at which the

respective row should normally be read (noted at the end of the row).

-> If pt reads at least 50% of the symbols on a row, the entire row is considered read

-> If pt misses more than 50% of the symbols on a row, then the previous line should be recorded as VA

When recording VA, it must be specified whether it is uncorrected (uc), corrected (cc), or pinhole (ph).

Additional steps for patients with low vision:

If pt cannot read the top row of the optotype (even with a pinhole), the following steps are taken:

-> Distance from the optotype is reduced by 1m until pt can read the first row (VA would then be =4/50, 3/50, 2/50 or 1/50),

considering that the first row must be read from 50m.

-> If pt still cannot read the first row of the optotype at 1m, we assess whether he can count the examiner's fingers

-> If pt cannot see to count the fingers, we assess whether he can see the movement of the examiner's hand

-> If pt does not perceive hand movements, we assess whether he perceives the light projected into his eyes from a

flashlight, in the dark room ("Light perception", L.P or "No light perception": NLP).

Measuring NEAR VA is performed using near optotypes.

(If pt normally uses glasses, we ensure that they wear them for the evaluation)

One eye is covered, and pt is invited to read the paragraph with the smallest letters they see. Repeat for the other eye.

Causes of decreased VA

1 . Refractive errors

2 . Amblyopia

3. Disorders of transparent media

4. Retina and optic nerve disorders

2. Visual field exam by confrontation method, detection of bitemporal & homonymous hemianopia

Visual field (VF) = everything that can be seen when pt fixates their gaze on a single point.

○ Several methods to measure it: some common methods include the use of specialized instruments (such as Humphrey

perimeter), capable of making sensitive measurements that can detect small defects throughout the VF.

○ Another less sensitive, but highly specific test, is known as the VF confrontation test = simple & quick to assess periph

vision without the use of expensive specialized equipment.

○ Indications of the VF confrontation test:

Whenever a condition that affects peripheral vision is suspected: glaucoma and other optic nerve conditions, retinal

detachment, stroke, retinal vascular occlusions, brain tumors.

○ Steps: (6)

1. Pt is asked to remove any hat or accessory that would interfere w/ peripheral vision

2 . Examiner positions himself in front of pt, ~1m away and the height of the chair is adjusted so that pt & examiner = at

the same level.

3. Pt is asked to lightly cover his left eye with his left hand and is instructed to fix his gaze directly on the examiner's left

eye throughout the test. Meanwhile, the examiner closes his right eye and maintains fixation on the patient's open eye.

4 . Examiner raises his hand at the lower temporal extremity of pt peripheral vision, halfway between the examiner and the

pt, showing 1, 2, or 5 fingers up. (Using only 1, 2 or 5 fingers helps pt to distinguish the nb easier.) Pt is asked how many

fingers he sees.

5. Step 4 is repeated, testing all 4 visual quadrants of the right eye: INF temporal, INF nasal, SUP temporal, & SUP nasal.

6. Steps 3, 4, and 5 are then repeated for the pt's left eye.

○ Test results:

☆ Bitemporal hemianopia= the absence of the temporal halves of the VF, with preservation of vision ONLY in the NASAL

halves of both eyes. It is caused by lesions of the MEDIAN portion of the optic chiasm, such as: pituitary tumors (inferior)

or craniopharyngioma (superior).

☆ Homonymous hemianopia (HH)= a VF defect involving either the two right halves or the two left halves of the VF of both

eyes. It is caused by damage to the RETROCHIASMATIC visual pathways = damage to the optic tract, lateral geniculate

nucleus, optic radiations, and cerebral (occipital) visual cortex.

Lesions located in the LEFT side of the brain produce RIGHT HH and lesions on the RIGHT side produce LEFT HH

⚠️

⚠️ There are patients with perfect visual acuity, but with significant VF changes

⚠️

3. Evaluation of color vision (= evaluation of chromatic sense)

○ Various subjective methods: (4)

Naming methods; Discrimination methods (pseudoisochromatic tests); Matching methods (anomaloscopes); Sorting

(arrangement) methods (Farnsworth tests)

1. Naming methods =

Based on the trichromatic theory of color perception stating that there are 3 fundamental colors (red, green, & blue), and

that the perception of color variety is d/t their mixing in ≠ proportions.

Pt is presented w/ images of various colors on a white background and he must indicate the color of each object

presented. Variants of this method involve presenting a test color and the patient must then choose the same color from a

set of colored plates.

Can dg patients with TOTAL ACHROMASIA (no color perception) and those with DICHROMASIA (perceive only 2/3 of the

fundamental colors)=> PROTANOPES (lack RED), DEUTERANOPES (lack GREEN), or TRITANOPES (lack BLUE).

2. Discrimination (confusion) method =

also based on trichromatic theory & performed using PSEUDOISOCHROMATIC tests

-> These contain a symbol (nb, letter, geometric shapes, animals, etc.) drawn in a certain color,

presented against a homogeneous or inhomogeneous colored background.

Most commonly used = Ishihara plates (with 14, 24 or 38 plates)

Can dg patients with PARTIAL color vision deficiencies= DYSCHROMATS

Dyschromat pt are called PROTANOMALOUS (difficulty seeing RED), DEUTERANOMALOUS (GREEN),

or TRITANOMALOUS (BLUE).

Pt may still recognize these colors when presented in isolation, on a white background!!!

⚠️

⚠️

3. Matching methods use a device called ANOMALOMETER

The patient is presented with a circular image, one half of which has a fixed reference color, and

the other half has a variable shade that the patient can adjust (using a dial) until it seems to him

to be the identical to the reference.

The most widely used is the Nägel anomalometer, in which the reference color is yellow. This is

obtained from a mixture of 50% red and 50% green; if the patient uses 70% red and 30% green, the

color he creates being more reddish than the reference, it means that he has difficulty perceiving

the color red. If, on the contrary, he uses more green, creating a greenish yellow, compared to the control, he has difficulty

perceiving the color green.

4. Sorting (arrangement) methods are based on the tetrachromatic theory of color perception, which assumes that all

colors are the result of combinations, in various proportions, of 4 fundamental colors distributed in 2 pairs of

complementary colors: red - green, and yellow - blue. These methods use Farnsworth tests, consisting of colored caps

labeled with numbers on the back. There are Farnsworth tests with 15 pieces (Farnsworth D15) and with 85 pieces

(Farnsworth Munsell 100Hue).

The patient must arrange the caps in the order of color hue progression. If correct, the caps will follow the numerical

sequence. The pieces can be placed directly on a circular surface. The tests have attached diagrams with 15 and 85

numbers, respectively, which will be joined in the order in which the patient placed the pieces.

The normal result is a circular diagram.

Errors produce line patterns oriented in certain directions, depending on the type of color vision defect

Why don't we have a simple computer-based color blindness test?

1. Computer screens use only 3 primary colors: red, green, and blue (RGB). Any other color is the result of mixing these

three colors. Anomaloscope and flashlight (naming) tests use different light sources that cannot be simulated by a display.

2. Each computer display has a different range of colors, slight differences in light sources, varying brightness, and more.

All of these are reflected in different test results. Only calibrated computers can be used to perform such computer tests.

To remember:

> Color perception assessment should be performed under standard lighting

conditions to minimize variability in results.

> The various tests for assessing color perception are suitable for different

purposes and levels of detail in the examinat°

> Some tests are better suited for screening, while others can provide more

detailed information about specific color deficiencies and their severity.

4. Pinhole test. Subjective examination of ocular refraction

Pinhole test:

Pinhole = a black, opaque disc with a round hole in the center.

Its role is to narrow the light beam, allowing it to pass only through the center of transparent media (especially the cornea

and lens), which are characterized by minimal refractive aberrations. There are pinhole spots with a single hole or with

multiple holes (advantage of mltpl = pt can find the hole through which to look more easily)

Purposes =

1. Differentiate the cause of

visual acuity (VA): refractive error versus organic ocular pathology.

If pt looks through the pinhole and :

☆ VA improves => REFRACTIVE error ; ☆ VA decreases => POST NUCLEAR/SUBCAPSULAR CATARACT or MACULAR path.

(age-related macular degenerat°, diabetic macular edema, etc...)

2. Measure VA in patients with drug-induced mydriasis

⬇️

Subjective examination of ocular refraction:

Equipment required: Optotype for distance; Occluder; Pinhole; Green's quadrant; Stenopeic slit

▪ Pt is seated 5 m away from the optotype and covers each eye alternately with an occluder or with the palm of their hand,

without pressing on the eye. The examiner shows pt one symbol per row, and if the patient reads at least 50% of the

symbols on a row, the entire row is considered read. There are different clinical scenarios:

1. A patient w/ VA=1 is considered:

☆ Emmetropic: using the pinhole does not produce any change

=> +0.50 dpt sph lens in front of the eye =

⬇️ VA -> This patient does NOT require optical correction.

☆ Hyperopia w/ Accommodative Amplitude (AcA) > or = to Hyperopia (HY): pinhole does not change the VA.

=> +0.50 dpt = VA maintained at 1 so the value is gradually

HM = value of previous lens

⬆️ by 0.50 dpt until VA decreases⬇️ [convergent spherical lens]

2. A patient w/ VA< 1 is considered:

☆ Hyperopic w/ AcA < HY: pinhole increases VA

=> + 0.50 dpt lens =

⬆️ VA, the value of the lens is gradually ⬆️ by 0.50 dpt until VA decreases⬇️ [convergent spherical lens]

HY = value of the previous lens

☆ Myopic: pinhole increases VA

⬇️ VA but with a lens -0.50 dpt = ⬆️ VA [divergent spherical lens]

Value is gradually ⬆️ by 0.50 dpt until VA=1 -> The value of myopia = the value of the lens

=> + 0.50 dpt =

☆ Astigmatic: pinhole increases VA

=> + 0.50 dpt =

⬇️ VA BUT - 0.50 dpt ALSO ⬇️ VA

Here, there are 2 methods, w/ the stenopeic slit and/or with the Green's quadrant:

○The use of the stenopeic slit improves VA on one axis.

The stenopeic slit is a black screen w/ a long slit in the center of a 1mm width: blocks most light

rays, allowing only those aligned with the slit orientation to pass. It is positioned in front of the

patient's eye and rotated.

For the eye w/ astigmatism, 2 positions are identified:

▪ One in which the VA is the best, indicating the position of the meridian closest to emmetropia and

▪ One in which the VA is the lowest, indicating the position of the most ametropic meridian.

To determine the value of the astigmatism, spherical + or - lenses are alternatively placed over the

slit in each meridian until maximum VA is achieved

Another method consists of rotating a cyl lens +0.50 dpt from 0° up to 180°, until the axis that

clarifies the image is found. After identifying the axis in which the image is clarified, the value of the

lens cylt is changed until the maximum VA is achieved. The same process is repeated w/ the lens

cyl -0.50 dpt.

○ Green's quadrant has rays on 180ºor 360°, pt perceives the rays that are parallel to the

emmetropic axis more clearly, while those seen more blurred correspond to the most astigmatic

axis.

To remember:

• The use of the pinhole allows for simple and rapid detection of refractive errors.

• The value of myopia is given by the weakest divergent lens with which the patient sees best.

• The value of hyperopia is given by the strongest convergent lens with which the patient sees best.

• Objective (using a retinoscope or autorefractor), Subjective (using a phoropter or stenopeic point) or Cycloplegic (using

cycloplegic drops) exam.

• Abnormal findings:

Myopia: Near objects can be seen clearly but distant objects are blurred: can be corrected using a concave (diverging) lens.

Hyperopia: Distant objects can be seen clearly but near objects are blurred: can be corrected w/ a convex (converging) lens.

Astigmatism: Cornea has a different shape, w/ meridians of different curvature, so the light rays reach different points on

retina. Cylinder/toric lenses are used.

5. Examinat° of ocular motility, detect° of strabismus (cover test), differentiat° btwn paralytic & nonparalytic strabismus

○ COVER test, which objective is to detect ocular deviations, can ONLY be performed on pt who have good visual acuity &

adequate concentration to look straight on a target object. Examiner's & patient's eyes should be at the same level.

▪ Pt looks straight at an object at 30 cm (near) and 6 meters (distance),

the movement of one of his eye is observed, the other eye is covered ▪

=> Eye that deviates spontaneously, w/out dissociation = manifest strabismus (concomitent or paralytic) = TROPIA

=> Eye that deviates only under dissociative conditions (bright light, fatigue, after cover test) = latent strabismus = PHORIA

○ MONOCULAR cover test (cover-uncover test):

▪ Pt looks straight at a distant or near target throughout the examination,

▪ The examiner, positioned slightly laterally and at arm's length from pt, covers one of the patient's eyes w/ a translucent

occluder/hand and observes the movement of the uncovered eye:

Does the eye change its position in order to take over fixation?

=> If the uncovered eye remains fixed (neither eye has changed its position), it may be either ORTHOPHORIA (no deviation),

or the covered eye is AMBLYOPIC (its input is suppressed centrally).

In such cases, the cover test has no indication and Hirschberg test* (see after) should be used instead.

▪ The covered eye is uncovered. Wait 2-3 seconds for binocular vision to be restored.

▪ Cover the other eye and observe the movements of the newly uncovered eye:

=> If the newly uncovered eye changes position to take on fixation, this indicates a HETEROTROPY (the type of deviation

depends on the direction of movement).

▪ Repeat the steps, this time observing the covered eye for the detection of any movement.

Clinical utility is to differentiate btwn a PHORIA and a TROPIA, and helps establish whether fixation is alternating or

monocular as follows:

☆ The uncovered eye will move in case of PHORIA

☆ In case of TROPIA, the eye w/ manifest strabismus does not move (remains deviated), while the fixating eye moves

upon uncovering

Fig.: Monocular cover test, after uncovering the left eye, a nasal deviation is observed

○ ALTERNATE cover test = based on the same principle but the examiner alternates covering each eye, without allowing

binocular fusion. Each occlusion lasts at least 3 seconds, and the movements should be rapid enough to dissociate fusion.

=> In case of TROPIA or PHORIA, there are eye movements when the other eye is covered.

=> In case of ORTHOPHORIA (normality), the alternating cover test is negative (no movement on uncovering).

Clinical utility is to confirms TROPIA and distinguishes btwn PHORIA & ORTHOPHORIA (normal) but it CANNOT

differentiate phoria from tropia.

*Hirschberg test

= Pt looks straight ahead (primary gaze), a light source will be projected, approximately 33 cm away from pt, to visualize

corneal reflexes in both eyes.

The position of the corneal light reflex is assessed relatively to the corneal center and deviation is expressed in degrees or

prism diopters -> Each mm of descentration = 7 degrees or 15 prismatic

diopters (PD).

Normally, an orthotropic patient (without spontaneous deviation) has

reflexes centered in the middle of the pupil.

Clinical utility here is to immediately detect a TROPIA, help estimate a

deviation and is useful in pt who are not compliant for the cover test or

who are amblyopic

Fig.: Hirschberg test: negative (normal)

○ Diagnosis of the paresis element in a heterotropia:

▪ Hx: Diplopia (acquired paresis also in adults), changes in eye positions, restrictions on eye movements

▪ Examination:

-> Monocular and binocular VA;

-> Compensatory head positions, ocular positions, palpebral fissure

-> Motility:

¤ Monocular (movement of one eye is examined, covering the other): movements are called DUCTIONS

¤ Binocular: movements in the SAME direction =VERSIONS, in the OPPOSITE direction =VERGENCES

Binocular motility is assessed in the 9 cardinal positions of gaze.

-> Refraction: especially in children with esotropia (manifest convergent strabismus)

-> Fundus examination (rotations of the macula: incyclo or excyclotorsion) (see table).

○ Ocular motility

examination:

Pt is seated with his eyes at

the same level as the

examiner's pointer and is

asked to follow the pointer

that the examiner moves in

the 9 directions of gaze:

primary position + up-downright-left-oblique directions.

The amplitude of the eye

movements is assessed, a

complete movement implies

the impossibility of

visualizing the sclera.

Table: Main differences between paralytic and non-paralytic strabismus

6. Examination of eyelids and conjunctiva with flashlight and slit lamp

1st part: Examination of the eyelids

Can be performed by macroscopic inspection in a well-lit room, ideally from a

maximum distance of 1m. Should also include eyebrow region (btwn frontalis &

orbicularis muscles), which plays an important role in supporting the eyelids.

For detailed analysis of lesions, slit lamp magnification is used, initially w/ diffuse illumination, then focal

illumination.

It examines:

▪ Position, shape and changes in the skin of the eyelids

▪ Eyebrow region, palpebral fissure and the free palpebral margin w/ the ANT (ciliary) & POST portions (drainage openings

of the Meibomian glds)

○ Shape and position anomalies:

☆ Entropion = Inward turning of the eyelid margin & eyelashes towards the globe causing friction injuries to the conjunctiva

and cornea, produced by cilia.

-> Causes:

▪ Involutional (most common, age-related)

▪ Cicatricial (scarring of palpebral conjunctiva) after chemical burns, lacerated conjunctival lesions, trachoma, StevensJohnson syndrome, ocular pemphigoid

▪ Spastic (excessive orbicularis oculi contraction: chronic conjunctivitis, keratitis)

▪ Congenital

☆ Ectropion = Outward turning of the eyelid margin, away from the globe.

-> Csq:

• Outward orientation of the inferior lacrimal punctum & loss of contact w/ the eyeball leads to epiphora & abrasions of the

skin around the eyelid;

• Chronic exposure of the conjunctiva leads to infection & keratinization; if advanced: keratitis & corneal ulceration

-> Causes:

▪ Involutional (age-related) – most common

▪ Cicatricial: chemical or thermal burns, trauma,

inflammation

▪ Congenital (rare, usually associated with

blepharophimosis syndrome)

▪ Mechanical: secondary to excision of a

chalazion or large tumors

☆ Trichiasis = misdirected eyelashes that rub against the cornea/conjunctiva, causing irritation and injury.

Can be primary or secondary to entropion.

-> Causes:

▪ Congenital

▪ Acquired: following scarring of the eyelid margin.

☆ Lagophthalmia = incomplete eyelid closure

Closure of the palpebral fissure is achieved by contraction of the orbicularis muscle, innervated by the facial nerve (VII).

-> Examination: pt is asked to close his eyes slightly, as if sleeping, observing whether the palpebral fissure closes

completely or not (leaves the conjunctiva/cornea exposed)

-> Causes: VII nerve palsy; Proptosis from thyroid eye disease; Coma

Fig.:

Left: Right eye lagophthalmia with paralytic ectropiona and widened palpebral fissure.

Right: when trying to close the eyes, an incomplete closure of the right eye is observed with exposure of the cornea and

palpebral conjunctiva.

☆ Floppy eyelid syndrome = Upper eyelid is flaccid & droopy, and can be easily everted

= Asso w/ papillary conjunctivitis on the upper tarsus.

☆ Blepharochalasis = Usually bilateral, characterized by loss of skin elasticity and atrophy of the subcutaneous tissue.

The eyelid skin hangs over the free palpebral margin.

☆ Dermatochalasis = Usually bilateral, characterized by loss of elasticity & atrophy of the skin and localized fat prolapse

(often nasal, upper lid).

☆ Ptosis (Blepharoptosis) = Upper eyelid is droopy, unilateral or bilateral, partially or completely.

The opening of the palpebral fissure is achieved by contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle (LPS),

innervated by oculomotor nerve (Ill).

-> Causes:

▪ Congenital (incomplete differentiation of LPS)

▪ Acquired: 3rd nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, myasthenia gravis, age-related

▪ Pseudoptosis is caused by eyelid edema, blepharochalasis

☆ Epicanthus (Mongoloid fissure) = Fold of skin at the inner corner of the eyelid, which gives an appearance of false

strabismus in newborns. It is present in Caucasians only in newborns, disappears with growth, but is characteristic of

Asians.

☆ Palpebral coloboma = Lack of tissue in the eyelids

○ Changes in the eyelid skin

☆ Contact dermatitis (irritative) includes eczematous lesions on the eyelid skin asso w/ palpebral edema & pruritus.

-> Causes: Most often caused by allergy to cosmetics, dye or topical drugs: neomycin, antiglaucomatous agents, atropine.

☆ Xanthelasma = Yellowish skin lesion, in the form of a plaque, slightly elevated, most often located at the medial portion

of the upper or lower eyelid.

☆ Hemangiomas = Bluish-reddish vascular lesions, localized at the skin level that may increase in size after the Valsalva

maneuver.

○ Changes in the eyebrow region

Height & shape of eyebrows are examined. Normally:

-> in MEN, eyebrows are at the same level w/ the upper edge of the orbit and are straight;

-> in WOMEN, eyebrows are located 1 cm above the upper edge of the orbit, slightly raised superiorly and laterally.

Eyebrow ptosis =distance measured from the middle of the upper eyelid to the lower edge of the eyebrow < 10 mm

○ Changes in the palpebral fissure

-> Examination:

▪ Pt is asked to look straight ahead in the primary position, distance in mm is measured from the middle of the free edge of

the upper eyelid to the middle of the free edge of the lower eyelid: N.V =9 mm (Caucasians)

=> NARROW in: Blepharoptosis, Pseudoptosis (blepharochalasis, palpebral edema, etc.), Anophthalmia, Enophthalmia

=> WIDE palpebral fissure in: Facial paresis, Lid retraction (thyroid eye disease -> Grave's).

○ Changes in the appearance of the free eyelid margin

☆ Blepharitis = Acute or chronic inflammation of the free eyelid margin.

-> Causes: Age (common in children), irritating factors (cosmetics, dust, cigarette

smoke), uncorrected refractive errors (excessive rubbing of the eyes to obtain a clear

image), infections, seborrheic skin, chronic conjunctivitis

-> Clinical forms:

▪ Erythematous: red, shiny lid margins

▪ Squamous: scaly deposits a t lash bases on erythematous background

▪ Ulcerative: ulcerations appear on the free edge, always of infectious etiology

(staphylococcal)

☆ Meibomitis = Chronic inflammation of meibomian glds, manifesting w/ whitish,

foamy secretions along the lid margin/canthus.

○ Other infections and inflammations of the eyelid

☆ Hordeolum = Acute, suppurative inflammation of a ciliary follicle, a Moll or a Zeiss gld, of staphylococcal etiology.

The lid is congested, swollen, w/ classic inflammatory signs, often with an ingrown lash, painful and warm to the touch.

☆ Chalazion = Chronic, inflammatory granuloma of the Meibomian glds

Presents as a firm, nodular, painless tumor formation,

located at lid margin, without inflammatory signs

○ Malignant eyelid tumors

☆ Basal cell carcinoma = most common malignant tumor

of the eyelid, most often located on the LOWER eyelid, in the

form of a pearly, ulcerative or indurated lesion.

☆ Squamous cell carcinoma appears as an ulcerative or

papillomatous nodule.

☆ Meibomian gld carcinoma appears as a discrete, firm, yellowish nodule and is often mistaken for a chalazion

Fig.: Tumor in the inner corner of the eyelid

2nd part: Examination of the conjunctiva

Examination w/ flashlight or in daylight provides rough information, which can still be useful.

The 3 portions of the conjunctiva must be inspected: bulbar, fornices, & palpebral (upper and lower).

Inspection of the palpebral conjunctiva and fornices is performed after everting the eyelids:

-> LOWER eyelid eversion: pt is asked to look upwards while the inf lid margin is pulled down w/ the thumb.

-> UPPER eyelid eversion: pt is asked to look down (without closing the eye), examiner grasp the eyelashes of the upper

eyelid btwn thumb and index, gently pulling the eyelid towards the examiner;

Then place the index finger of the left hand on the upper eyelid, approximately 5-10 mm from the lid margin, and gently

press down the eyelid already stretched by lash traction. (A cotton swab or a special tool can be used).

Slit lamp examination of the conjunctiva is performed by diffuse or focal illumination with magnification.

Transparency and color are analyzed, as well as the presence of pathological changes: congestion, edema, secretions,

follicles, papillae, nodules, foreign bodies, degenerative lesions, ulcerations, cysts, hemorrhages.

○ Transparency changes

Normally, through the transparency of the conjunctiva, the sclera & tarsal glds can be visualized.

=> Scarring of the conjunctiva leads to the loss of its transparency, d/t its replacement w/ a white fibrous tissue.

Almost all pathological changes encountered in the conjunctiva lead to the loss of transparency: congestion, edema, ...

○ Color changes

Conjunctiva = transparent SO its color = chges in underlying tissues (sclera, vessels, ...). Conjunctival:

▪ PALLOR => Anemia, After giving vasoconstrictors, Burns

▪ XANTHOSIS (yellowish)

=> Jaundice

▪ CYANOSIS =>

Generalized cyanosis

▪ BLACKISH color =>

Melanin deposits, scleral

staphyloma (uvea is

visible through the thin

sclera).

▪ Bitot's spots (WHITISH)

=> Vitamin A deficiency

▪ REDDISH => Congestion

/ Subconjunctival

hemorrhage

○ Conjunctival congestion

(may involve conjunctival,

anterior ciliary or episcleral vessels)

▪ Conjunctival vessel congestion = Peripherally [=Superficial] (includes upper & lower palpebral conjunctiva, fornices and

bulbar conjunctiva up to 3-4 mm from the limbus), has a bright RED color and disappears with vasoconstrictor.

Most common cause = conjunctivitis, in which case discharge is also present

▪ Anterior ciliary vessel congestion = Centrally, surrounding the cornea circumferentially for approximately 3-4 mm

(perikeratic ring), is PURPLE and does NOT disappear with vasoconstrictor.

Occurs in: Keratitis, Iridocyclitis, Acute glaucoma

▪ Episcleral vascular congestion = Peripherally located, bright RED, vessels anastomose in a "medusa head" pattern, and

turns WHITE when using vasoconstrictor. Occurs in: Absolute glaucoma & Raised episcleral venous pressure

○ Conjunctival edema and chemosis

The laxity & rich vascularity of the conjunctiva creates optimal conditions for fluid accumulation, most often in the bulbar

conjunctiva (where the conjunctiva is laxer).

=> Chemosis = conjunctival edema so pronounced that it herniates through the palpebral fissure.

-> Causes: Severe acute infectious conjunctivitis, membranous conjunctivitis, angioneurotic edema, drug reaction, allergic

conjunctivitis, postoperative.

○ Formation of membranes and adhesions in the conjunctiva

Membranes form from fibrin exudation from hyperpermeable conjunctival vessels and occurs in severe forms of bacterial

& viral conjunctivitis, but also in drug reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. It is classified into :

☆ TRUE conjunctival mb: Removed w/ difficulty, leaving bleedings behind, d/t the extension into the conjunctival epith

☆ PSEUDOmembranes: more superficial, extending only on the surface, not into the epithelium: Removed easily, w/ a lower

risk of bleeding

=> The Symblepharon = condition w/ abnormal adhesions btwn the palpebral &

bulbar conjunctiva

-> Causes: Chemical (most often alkali) and thermal burns, membranous

conjunctivitis, cicatricial ocular pemphigoid.

○ Follicles = csq of a lymphoid reaction following a viral, chlamydial conjunctival

injury, irritating agents or drugs that manifest as small, pale hemispherical nodules

(~Grains of rice) on the palpebral conjunctiva & fornices.

-> Causes: Viral /caused by Chlamydia conjunctivitis (swimming pool

conjunctivitis), less commonly drug reactions.

○ Papillae = Nodular formations larger than follicles, w/ same location, red (vascularized), (~ Paving stones/crocodile skin)

-> Causes: Allergic and bacterial conjunctivitis. By size, the papillae are :

☆ SMALL (1-2 mm): Allergic/ Bacterial conjunctivitis

☆ GIANT (over 2 mm): in contact lens and ocular prosthesis wearers

○ Conjunctival secretions (discharge) = made of tears, mucus & inflammatory

cells, fibrin, pus.

Its appearance is very important toestablish the dg:

▪ WATERY = Allergic, viral conjunctivitis, ▪ MUCOID = Chronic dacryocystitis, ▪

PURULENT = Bacterial conjunctivitis,

▪ VISCOUS = Vernal conjunctivitis

○ Subconjunctival hemorrhage = Accumulation of blood under the conjunctiva

-> Causes: Traumatic, after Valsalva maneuver, skull base fracture, hypertensive

crisis, purpura, ...

○ Conjunctival degenerations: Pinguecula and pterygium

☆ Pinguecula appears in adults in the form of a nodule located at the palpebral fissure, near the limbus, but without

corneal invasion caused by elastoid degeneration of conjunctival collagen

☆ Pterygium = degeneration that also affects cornea & conjunctiva, which appears after 40y, most often located medially,

in the form of a triangular fold with the tip towards the cornea, with a tendency to progression

Fig.:Pterygium

○ Conjunctival nodules of various etiologies, shapes and sizes, occur most often at the limbus.

Causes differ depending on the location from the limbus:

▪ Near = Phlycten, dermoid cyst, filtering bleb; ▪ Away = Dermolipoma, granuloma, conjunctival cysts

○ Pigmented congenital lesions: Conjunctival nevi, conjunctival melanosis

○ Tumor lesions:

☆ BENIGN: Conjunctival papillomas, keratoacanthomas;

☆ MALIGNANT: Carcinoma

Fig: Conjunctival carcinoma

7. Examination of the cornea. Testing corneal sensitivity

▪ The cornea is both the first lens of the eye, providing ~ 2/3 of its refractive power, and a protective covering, being part of

the outer tunic of the eyeball, along w/ the sclera. ~ shape of a spherical cap, w/ a diameter of 11.5-12.5 mm.

▪ Properties= Luster, transparency & sensitivity

▪ The adnexa (eyelids, lacrimal system) constantly protect and cleanse it

▪ A rich network of free nerve endings, branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, innervates the surface

of the cornea and makes it 100x more sensitive than the surrounding tissues, triggering the corneal reflex (blinking) when

an external factor irritates it.

○ Examination of the cornea:

= Examined with the naked eye, using lateral illumination, and in more detail with the slit lamp.

☆ Dimensions: Megalocornea =diameter ≥ 13 mm and may signal congenital glaucoma

☆ Luster: Corneal surface behaves like a mirror, ensured by epithelial integrity.

-> Loss of luster and a matte appearance suggest epithelial defects => to confirm corneal epithelial loss, fluorescein

staining is performed

☆ Transparency = maintained by perfect parallelism of stromal fibers, cst hydration, and absence of vascularization.

-> Loss of transparency may occur in scarring, inflammation (keratitis), increased intraocular pressure, or corneal neovascu.

☆ Corneal sensitivity examination =

Corneal sensitivity can be tested with an aesthesiometer, a procedure usually used only in clinical trials or commonly

assessed using a sterile cotton tip touching the cornea in 4 quadrants (which are divided by 2 perpendicular axes passing

through the center of the cornea, horizontally and vertically).

Sensitivity is compared btwn the quadrants and then with that of the unaffected eye.

⚠️ Skin sensitivity is also tested in the territory of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve that includes the cornea

(palpebral skin, forehead), by light touches, comparing it w/ the sensitivity of the contralateral skin.

-> In neurotrophic keratitis (destruction of corneal innervation): hypoesthesia (generally in all quadrants) and corneal

anesthesia are observed.

-> If the trigeminal involvement = located in the area of the Gasser ganglion, cutaneous sensitivity is also affected

To remember:

♡ if Megalocornea, congenital glaucoma must be ruled out

♡ Corneal luster = decreased in corneal epithelial defects

♡ Corneal transparency = decreased in keratitis, corneal scarring, intraocular htn, corneal neovascularization

♡ Sensitivity = diminished/absent in neurotrophic keratitis

8. Fluorescein staining

○ Indication: Whenever corneal epithelial lesions, traumatic or inflammatory, are suspected

○ Properties of fluorescein

▪ Fluorescein is an orange dye, derived from a resin. It has a large molecule, so it will not be able to penetrate the intact

corneal epithelium that functions as a barrier, which is why it will not stain a normal cornea

=> If the epithelium is missing, fluorescein adheres to the stroma and stains it GREEN.

▪ Fluorescein absorbs light in the blue spectrum (490 nm) and emits yellow-green light w/ a longer wavelength (530 nm),

therefore the staining can be seen more easily if a cobalt blue filter is used.

Although fluorescein stains the de-epithelialized cornea very effectively, it is more difficult to detect fluorescein staining of

the conjunctiva because of poor scleral contrast.

○ Required

▪ Fluorescein eye drops or individual sterile paper strips impregnated w/ fluorescein

▪ Can be performed in daylight, using lateral illumination

▪ In the ophthalmology office, it is performed using a slit lamp, preferably equipped w/ a cobalt blue filter

○ Stages of examination

▪ Fluorescein is either instilled into the conjunctival sac or strips of paper impregnated with dye are applied to the bottom

of the lower conjunctival sac

▪ Pt is asked to blink several times to allow the dye to distribute evenly across the surface of the cornea

▪ Cornea is examined (using lateral illumination or a slit lamp w/ the cobalt blue filter)

○ Interpretation

▪ If areas that are impregnated w/ green color are identified on the corneal surface, the result is POSITIVE, signifying the

existence of de-epithelialization.

=> In superficial herpetic keratitis, appearance of the lesion = pathognomonic, having the shape of a dendritic branch or

geographic map

▪ If no green-stained area is identified on the corneal surface, the result is NEGATIVE = INTEGRITY of the corneal epithelium

+4 uses (not in the book)

9. Detection of abnormal pupil: color, shape, contour, position, diameter

The pupil = opening in the center of the iris.

Normally, the pupil is black in direct light & red in reflected light. It is round, relatively central (0.5 mm inferonasal to the

center of the iris), w/ a diameter btwn 2 and 4 mm under normal lighting conditions

○ Abnormalities of pupil color

▪ WHITE pupil = the most common color change of the pupil = LEUKOCORIA

Although its presence can be assessed without dilating the pupil, it is much more clearly seen after mydriasis

-> Causes:

☆ Retinoblastoma = malignant tumor of the retina, mainly affecting children< 3yo

☆ Mature cataract = complete opacification of the lens

☆ Pupillary occlusion = obstruction by the presence of a fibrinous pupillary mb (context of severe uveitis)

☆ Persistence of fetal vascularization = rare congenital anomaly in which hyaloid blood vessels do not regress completely,

▪ YELLOWISH pupil is seen in endophthalmitis

○ Abnormalities of pupil shape

▪ Oval, vertically elongated pupil in Acute angle closure glaucoma

The marked increase in intraocular pressure determines ischemia of the iris sphincter and its dysfunction

Result = Deformation of the pupil being in fixed semi-mydriasis (it no longer reacts to light)

▪ "Keyhole- shaped" pupil in iris coloboma (" Coloboma" =lack of tissue d/t dvp defect during intrauterine period)

= Lack of formation of the lower sector of the iris, so that the pupil extends inferiorly, having the appearance of a "keyhole".

Always inferiorly because the closure of the optic fissure is achieved inferiorly.

Can be uni- or bilateral, isolated or associated w/ other ocular anomalies (chorioretinal or optic nerve colobomas)

▪ A D-shaped pupil = sign of iridodialysis (disinsertion of the iris root)

The edge of the pupil becomes straight in the sector of iridodialysis, but remains round where the iris root is attached.

○ Abnormalities of pupil contour

▪ POST IRIS SYNECHIAE = peripupillary irido-crystalline adhesions that can occur in anterior uveitis and pull on the pupillary

margin, leading to its deformation

▪ RUPTURES of the iris sphincter (post-traumatic): pupil has a jagged outline

○ Abnormalities of pupil location

▪ CORRECTOPIA = Eccentric location of the pupil. It can be congenital or acquired (Trauma, iris tumors, ophthalmic surgery)

○ Abnormalities of pupil diameter

= Always examined before administering eye drops, under conditions of equal illumination of both pupils.

▪ MIOSIS = REDUCTION of the pupillary diameter < 2mm

☆ Unilateral miosis in: iritis, keratitis or sympathetic paralysis

(Claude Bernard-Horner synd complete triad = ipsilateral miosis, ptosis, enophthalmos).

☆ Bilateral miosis in: irritative neurological lesions of the meninges (hemorrhages, meningitis), craniocerebral trauma (less

serious prognosis than mydriasis), or poisoning (uremic coma, opiate, nicotine or barbiturate poisoning).

▪ MYDRIASIS = INCREASE of pupillary diameter > 4 mm

☆ Unilateral mydriasis after ocular or cranial trauma, in unilateral blindness, or in case of oculomotor nerve paralysis

☆ Bilateral mydriasis in: complete blindness, head trauma, or various endogenous/exogenous intoxications

▪ ANISOCORIA = UNEQUAL diameter of the 2 pupils. Pupillary diameter is evaluated in both light and dark.

Not all cases of anisocoria are considered pathological; ~ 10-20% of the general pop has physiological anisocoria

10. Testing pupillary reflexes

= Very important in the ophthalmological and neurological examination. 3 pupillary reflexes are evaluated:

☆ DIRECT light reflex => Ability of the pupil to react by constriction to the projection of a light stimulus in its direction.

Testing method:

Exam is performed in low light conditions, with pt asked to fixate at distance.

For example, pt is asked to sit in a chair in front of the optotype and to look at the largest symbol while its light remains on

and the room lights are off.

Examiner = to the side of the patient to not obstruct fixation at a distance [bc if the patient looks at the examiner (or fixes

an object at close range), the accommodation-convergence- miosis reflex (see below) intervenes, which interferes with the

assessment of photomotor reflexes]

Examiner uses a light directed in front of the tested pupil from ~10 cm for ~3 sec. The light beam should be perpendicular

to the pupillary area (including if the patient has strabismus), but without stimulating the contralateral pupil.

Each eye is tested separately.

Normal response = prompt constriction

=> Absence or delay of pupillary constriction suggests optic nerve damage or extensive retinal patho in the respective eye.

☆ CONSENSUAL light reflex => Ability of the CONTRALATERAL pupil to react by constriction

Testing method: Examination conditions are the same as for direct photomotor reflex testing.

Light is projected in front of one pupil, but this time the constriction of the contralateral pupil is assessed.

Normally, the contralateral pupil reacts by promptly constricting, simultaneously with the stimulated pupil.

This photomotor response is explained by the bilateral projection of afferent fibers to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei.

(2 Edinger-Westphal nuclei in the midbrain - one on the right, one on the left. Each nucleus receives afferent fibers from both eyes, but emits

parasympathetic efferent fibers with a strictly ipsilateral disposition, which reach the eyeball via the oculomotor nerve.)

=> Absence or delay may indicate brainstem involvement or oculomotor nerve damage.

☆ Accommodation-convergence-miosis reflex (TRIPLE reflex)=> Constrict° for near vision + accommodat° + convergence

Testing method: Examination is performed in a well-lit room. Pt is asked to fixate at a distance (eg. look at first row of

optotype), then to change fixation to near (eg. look at the tip of a pen held close to the patient's nose).

Normally, miosis & convergence are observed when the patient fixes near.

11. Testing the red pupillary reflex and recognition of leukocoria.

○ PUPILLARY RED REFLEX (fundus reflex) = Reflective phenomenon observed when light entering the pupil is reflected

back by the retina, creating a reddish-orange glow. (Can also be observed in flash photography)

Condition for light to reach the retina = that the ocular media be transparent.

=> Clinically: Important especially in children, starting from the neonatal period.

Fig: Normal bilateral pupillary red reflex

○ Variations in appearance according to skin color

▪ Fair skin: RED ▪ Moderately dark skin: ORANGE ▪ Dark skin: GREENISH, BLUISH

○ Required materials: Ophthalmoscope; Mydriatic drops; Darkend room

○ Examination steps

Exam is performed in a dark room so that the red pupillary reflex is easier to see. Eyes of pt & examiner at the same level.

Examiner sits in front of the patient, ~ 50 cm away, holding the ophthalmoscope close to the eye. Pt look into the light.

Ophthalmoscope light is directed towards each eye separately, assessing the individual pupillary red reflex.

Direct the light of the ophthalmoscope towards both eyes simultaneously to assess the symmetry of the red reflex.

○ Interpretation

Must be observed: presence/absence, color, brightness, symmetry btwn the 2 eyes.

=> Leukocoria (white pupil) means a pale, white or yellowish fundus reflex, and is caused by the reflection of light by

another structure: tumor (retinoblastoma), cataract.

=> Asymmetry = caused by strabismus, anisometropia: reflex appears weaker in the affected eye.

To remember:

• It is advisable to examine the pupillary red reflex in all patients in the neonatal period, as well as at subsequent routine

check-ups: Any abnormalities

discovered, especially

leukocoria, require urgent referral

to an ophthalmologist.

12. Digital tonometry

Digital tonometry or palpation =

method of estimating

intraocular pressure by gently

pressing with the index finger

on the closed eye.

▪ Execution: examiner uses the 2

index fingers, alternatively, to

palpate the sclera, through the

closed eyelids

▪ Clinical utility: Palpation

provides a rough estimate of

intraocular pressure, not an exact

value.

= very useful in the case of large variations in IOP, either in the direction of increase (acute glaucoma) or decrease

(perforation of the eyeball) -> Marked increase is palpated as a "rock-hard" sensation.

☆ Acute angle closure glaucoma: palpation to differentiate an acute glaucoma attack from other conditions that progress

with a red, painful eye and

⬇️ VA, such as iridocyclitis.

☆ Congenital glaucoma: helps differentiate from other causes of red and watery eyes, such as neonatal conjunctivitis and

nasolacrimal duct imperforation

=> A marked decrease in IOP = a sign of:

• Ocular perforation

• Choroidal detachment

• Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

13. Use of the ophthalmoscope for examination of the fundus and detection of the normal optic disc

○ Definition and importance of back of the eye's examination

Back of the eye's exam = called ophthalmoscopy, and the instrument used =ophthalmoscope.

Ophthalmoscopy is mandatory in the examination of any patient, as it allows dg of diseases affecting the retina, optic

nerve or choroid. Also extremely important for pt w/ general conditions (diabetes, HTN, kidney disease, etc.).

○ Examination steps

▪ Before the exam, mydriasis is required and achieved using parasympatholytic agents (Tropicamide 0.5-1%) &

sympathomimetic agents (Phenylephrine) and ophthalmoscopy is performed in a dark room.

(In pt w/ diabetes, prior cataract surgery, or hx of anteuveitis, mydriasis may be more difficult to obtain bc not all of

the retina is accessible for examination and the extreme periphery of the retina cannot be examined.)

▪ Direct ophthalmoscopy is performed using a direct ophthalmoscope: consists of a handle and

an optical system that projects light onto the retina. This system allows focusing of light on the

retina using a complex of lenses and adjustment of light properties. White or red-free (green)

light can be used, green being more useful for retinal blood vessels.

▪ Examiner projects the ophthalmoscope light into the patient's pupil from a distance of 30-40 cm to assess the red reflex.

Its presence indicates clear ocular media (cornea, aqueous humor, lens, vitreous), while its absence or alteration suggests

pacification of these media or certain retinal pathologies (e.g. retinoblastoma).

▪ Ophthalmoscope is then brought closer, to about 3-5 cm from the eye, until retinal details can be visualized. Examination

is monocular: examiner's right eye = used to examine patient's right eye (left eye for left eye).

The light beam is directed in multiple directions to explore as much of the retina as possible. By rotating the diopter

adjustment dial, image clarity is optimized.

The optic nerve (ON), retina & blood vessels are examined.

▪ Retina = red

▪ ON head (opt disc) =pink-yellow, clearly delimited from surrounding retina & slightly nasally to post pole

▪ Posterior pole is marked by the fovea (darker area in the central macula).

▪ At the center of the optic disc lie the trunk and initial branches of the retinal vessels

☆ Normal appearance of ON in direct ophthalmoscopy (must be interpreted w/ full clinical picture & complemented by other exams)

Through direct ophthalmoscopy, initial segment of the ONH is visualized, also called the optic disc (OD) d/t its round

appearance. Once the optic disc is identified, its characteristics are evaluated: contour, color, and cup ("the 3Cs").

♡ Contour: normal = sharp & well defined, lying in the same plane as the retina.

=> Blurred margins suggest optic disc edema (stasis, inflammation, or ischemia).

♡ Color: normal = "doughnut" = pink-orange color (= good neuroretinal perfusion) w/ a pale center.

=> Pale OD = optic atrophy (optic neuropathies, advanced glaucoma, or ischemic optic events)

=> Hyperemic (reddish) OD = inflammation of ONH

♡ Cup : Pale central zone of the "pink-orange doughnut" =physiological cup, representing the absence of neuroretinal tissue

in this area -> Clinically important parameter = Cup-to-disc ratio (vertical cup diameter / disc diameter) normal if <0.3

=> Increased ratio = pathognomonic sign of chronic glaucoma, reflecting loss of healthy neuroretinal rim tissue.

☆ Dimensions: ONH can be slightly variable (constitutional factors, refractive errors).

=> in HYPEROPIA (especially above +3 dpt), OD is smaller bc the eye is also smaller. OD = more hyperemic + slightly

prominent because the OD fibers end up "crowded" into a smaller OD.

=> In MYOPIA, OD is larger, and often surrounded by areas of peripapillary retinal atrophy

Fig: Normal appearance of OD when examined with a direct ophthalmoscope

☆ HYPERTENSIVE RETINOPATHY

Primary response of retinal arterioles to systemic HTN = vasoconstriction which allows clinical

classification into:

▪ Grade 1 : mild and generalized narrowing of the retinal arterioles

▪ Grade 2 : focal narrowing of the arterioles, Salus sign (when an artery

crosses a vein, w/ vein giving the impression of bending slightly at the AV crossing), Bonnet sign (when the segment of the vein distal to the AV

▪ Grade 3: Grade 2 + retinal hemorrhages + hard exudates, sometimes arranged in a "macular star"

+ cotton-wool spots

▪ Grade 4: Severe grade 3 + optic disc edema, marker of "malignant" hypertension

15. Use of the ophthalmoscope for detection of papilledema, glaucomatous cupping, and optic atrophy

☆ Papilledema: Definition and Ophthalmoscopic Appearance

Papilledema = swelling of the optic disc -> Multiple causes, classified into 2 broad categories:

▪ Increased intracranial pressure (

○

⬆️ ICP) = True papilledema ; or

▪ Optic nerve diseases

⬆️ ICP causes stasis papillary edema either:

- ACUTE papillary edema:

Bilateral elevated OD, hyperemic, w/ blurred edges, obstruction of blood vessel visibility at this level, venous congestion,

retinal or peripapillary "flame-shapped" haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots.

⚠️ Visual acuity = NORMAL, but there is an enlargement of the physiological blind spot

- CHRONIC papillary edema:

OD acquires a more grayish color, the cotton-wool spots, retinal hemorrhages and

hyperemia disappear.

Finally, progressive loss of the visual field, central visual acuity occurs, and optic

atrophy sets in.

○ Optic neuropathies main feature =swelling of the OD d/t either inflammation

(anterior optic neuritis or papillitis) or ischemia (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

-AION, non-arteritic or arteritic).

▪ Anterior optic neuritis: unilateral edematous optic disc, hyperemic, w/ blurred

edges, usually without peripapillary hemorrhages; visual impairment may be subtle

or profound, associated relative

afferent pupillary defect (RAPD +).

▪ Non-arteritic AION : paler swelling

of OD (often segmental, superior or

inferior part), blurred margins,

flame- shaped hemorrhages,

moderate visual loss; optic atrophy

without excavation (segmental or

diffuse) after edema resolution

Examination of the fellow eye may reveal a more congested disc, with a small or

absent C/D ratio

▪ Arteritic AION : pale, chalky white papillary edema, sometimes w/ "flame shaped"

hemorrhages, narrower retinal arterioles; occasionally, a concomitant occlusion of the central retinal artery may occur;

associated with systemic symptoms + increased ESR/CRP

○ Optic atrophy: definition and ophthalmoscopic appearance

= Degeneration of the optic nerve fibers, leading to pallor and thinning of the optic nerve head, with irreversible vision

impairment

▪ Causes: optic nerve compression, pre-existing papilledema, primary or secondary glaucoma, alcohol/methanol

consumption, vitamin B12 deficiency

▪ Main changes in the optic disc :

♡ PALLOR of the OD (especially temporal in demyelinating forms)

♡ Reduction of peripapillary vascularity (narrowed arterioles);

♡ Clear edges of the optic disc (unlike papilledema, in which they are blurred); increased cupping (in glaucoma)

♡ Peripapilary atrophy (whitish areas around the optic disc)

○ Glaucoma: definition and ophthalmoscopic appearance

= Progressive optic neuropathy characterized by damage to optic nerve fibers, asso w/ elevated intracular pressure (IOP).

Optic disc changes are essential in diagnosis and monitoring.

Main changes of the ON seen in glaucoma =

a. Increased optic disc cupping:

⬆️ cup-to-disc ratio (C/D), (vertical cup diam / disc diam); the closer the value is to 1, the more advanced the lesions are.

b . Asymmetry between the two eyes (C/D difference > 0.2 = suggestive of glaucoma)

c . Thinning of the neural rim (reduction of the neuroretinal rim)

In most healthy eyes = characteristic configuration of the neuroretinal rim called the "ISNT" rule:

Thickness is greatest: Inferior, then Superior>Nasal>and narrowest = Temporal

=> Glaucoma is characterized by progressive narrowing of the neuroretinal rim, more pronounced INF and SUP

d. Optic disc hemorrhages:

=> Presence of flame-shaped hemorrhages at the edge of papilla = RF for glaucoma & sign of inadequate disease control

e. Temporal peripapillary atrophy

Can be differentiated into 2 zones (a and ß) located most frequently in the infero-temporal region:

a-zone = External and ß-zone = Internal, adjacent to the edge of the optic disc

f. Nasal displacement of the central retinal vessels - their trajectory is oriented along the nasal wall of the excavation
